title: Sentence completion: making sound effects for films

segments.speaker: N
segments.text: You will hear a sound effects artist called Rosa Field talking about her work in films.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Hello, everyone, and thank you for having me. My job title is Foley artist. That means I create the everyday sounds you hear in films. Footsteps, doors closing, the rustle of a coat as someone sits down.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Very few of those sounds are recorded on set. The microphones on set are there for the actors' voices. Everything else is added later, in a studio, by people like me.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: People often assume I trained in music, or perhaps in the theatre. In fact, I started out at a small radio station. I was making tea and answering the phones.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: One day, the man who did the sound effects for a radio drama was ill. There was nobody else around, so I was asked to help.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: The first sound I ever made was a fire. Not a real fire, of course. Most beginners crumple a sheet of paper for that, but it sounds rather dull. I was shown how to use a sheet of cellophane instead.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: You squeeze it slowly, close to the microphone, and it crackles remarkably like flames. I was hooked from that moment.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: These days, I work mostly on feature films. Each film takes me about six weeks. Sorry, I should say eight weeks. Six was the old schedule, before digital editing made directors so much more demanding.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: So what is the most important sound I make? Not explosions, and not doors, although I do plenty of both. It's footsteps.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Audiences rarely notice them. But if they're missing, a scene feels strangely empty, and nobody can say why. I own over two hundred pairs of shoes for this purpose. My partner jokes that the shoes have their own bedroom. That's only slightly untrue.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: The surface matters just as much as the shoe. In our studio, the floor is divided into squares. There's concrete, wood, gravel, and even a shallow pool of water.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Wood is easy. Concrete is easy. Gravel is by far the hardest to get right. If you walk on it a fraction too heavily, it sounds like someone eating breakfast cereal.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Some sounds come from very unexpected objects. For a scene with breaking bones, we don't go anywhere near a hospital. For softer injuries, a cabbage works well. But for bones, I use celery.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: You twist a stick of fresh celery right next to the microphone, and the result is horribly convincing. I can't eat it any more, to be honest.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: People often ask me whether computers will replace us. There are enormous libraries of recorded sounds now. They're very useful for things like traffic or rain.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: But a library can't match an actor's movements exactly. Every actor walks differently. Some drag their feet. Some bounce. So we watch the screen and perform in time with them.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: A colleague of mine describes our work as a kind of dance. I see why, but I'd put it differently. Good Foley is really a kind of acting. You have to understand the character before you can give them a sound.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: If you're thinking about this career, my advice is simple. Don't spend a fortune on equipment, and don't rush into an expensive course.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Start by listening. Sit in a café, close your eyes, and try to name every sound you hear. That habit, more than anything else, is what trained my ears.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Right. I've brought a bag of shoes and a bunch of celery with me. Shall we make some noise?
